verdict.rationale: Across the anchor texts the grammar makes God or the Spirit the sole acting agent of the new birth and the person the recipient. The verb 'to beget or be born' (gennao) stands in the passive throughout John 3, namely 'might be born' (gennethe, a completed past action in passive voice in the subjunctive mood, so 'should be born'), and 'that which has been born' (gegennemenon, a completed action whose result still stands, in passive voice as a participle). The same pattern appears in John 1:13 with 'they were born' (egennethesan, a completed past action in passive voice as a simple statement of fact) and in 1 John with 'has been born' (gegennetai, a completed action whose result still stands, in passive voice as a simple statement of fact). John 1:13 negates three human sources of the birth in a row (not of bloods, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of a man) before the single positive 'from God' (ek theou). Where the verb is active the subject is God: 'he made alive together with' (synezoopoiesen) in Ephesians 2:5 of those who were dead, 'he saved' (esosen) in Titus 3:5 after denying works we did, 'having begotten again' (anagennesas) in 1 Peter 1:3, and 'having willed, he brought forth' (bouletheis apekuesen) in James 1:18. Ezekiel 36 stacks first person divine verbs ('to give', natan; 'to remove', sur; 'to do or bring about', asah; all in the 'I' form) ahead of the second person human response verbs. The agency claim is therefore lexically decisive. The stricter sub-claim that the new birth is logically prior to and the cause of faith is a defensible inference from the enabling language of John 6:65 (no one is able to come unless it has been given), but the words state dependence rather than an explicit 'order of salvation' (ordo salutis), so overall confidence is medium rather than high.

scripture.force: The verb 'might be born' (gennethe) parses as a completed past action in passive voice in the subjunctive mood (a 'might' or 'should' form), third person singular, so the person is born, not the one who does the birthing. The adverb 'from above, or again' (anothen) marks the source as upper, not human. The negated 'is able' (dynatai, ongoing simple statement of fact) in 'cannot see the kingdom of God' makes entry depend on undergoing the birth. The grammatical subject of the begetting is left open and the surrounding discourse supplies the Spirit.

Twice 'that which has been born' (gegennemenon) stands as a perfect passive participle (a completed action whose result still stands, in passive voice), once 'from the flesh' (ek tes sarkos) and once 'from the Spirit' (ek tou pneumatos), so flesh begets flesh and Spirit begets spirit. The perfect passive frames the begotten one as the settled result of an action done to it, and the two 'from' (ek) phrases keep the originating source outside the one born.

The wind or Spirit (pneuma) blows 'where it wills' (hopou thelei, third person singular present active of 'to will', thelo, an ongoing simple statement of fact), and the perfect passive participle 'one who has been born' (gegennemenos, a completed action whose result still stands, in passive voice) describes everyone born of the Spirit. The willing belongs to the Spirit and the person is the patient, an analogy of an origin that is real but not at human disposal.

The Spirit is the one that gives life ('giving life', zoopoioun, an ongoing-action participle in the active voice) and the flesh profits nothing ('nothing', ouden). Life-giving is assigned to the Spirit and explicitly denied to the sphere of the flesh, locating the source of spiritual life outside human capacity.

'No one' (oudeis) 'is able' (dynatai, an ongoing simple statement of fact) to come to me 'unless' (ean me, an 'if-then' style conditional clause) it 'has been given' (dedomenon, a perfect passive participle of 'to give', didomi, marking a completed action whose result still stands, in passive voice) to him from the Father. The negated capacity plus the conditional perfect-passive gift places the enabling act prior to and as the ground of the coming, which is the lexical basis for the priority sub-claim.

A chain of first person verbs governs the verse. 'To give' (natan) stands as first common singular (the 'I' form: 'I will give a new heart and a new spirit') and 'to remove' (sur) as a hiphil first common singular (the Hebrew causative form, 'to cause to do', in the 'I' form: 'I will remove the heart of stone'). Yahweh is the only subject of the transforming verbs and the people are the recipients, with no human verb of contribution in the giving.

I will put 'my Spirit' (ruchi, from ruach, 'spirit' or 'breath'; the verb 'to give', natan, in the first common singular, the 'I' form) within you and 'I will bring it about' ('to do', asah, first common singular, the 'I' form) that you walk in my statutes. The divine first person verbs come first and the human response verbs that follow (you will keep, you will walk, you will do) are all second person, so the morphology (word-form analysis) itself orders cause before effect.

While we were dead ('being dead', ontas nekrous, an ongoing-state participle of 'to be' plus the adjective 'dead', nekros) in trespasses, God 'made us alive together' (synezoopoiesen, a completed past action in active voice as a simple statement of fact, third person singular) with Christ, by grace. The compound 'made alive together with' (syn-zoopoieo) is rare (only here and Colossians 2:13), and the active verb has God as subject acting on those whose state is described as dead, so the dead do not contribute to their own being-made-alive.

'Not' (ouk) from works in righteousness that 'we did' (a completed past action in active voice as a simple statement of fact, first person plural), but according to his 'mercy' (eleos) 'he saved us' (esosen, a completed past action in active voice as a simple statement of fact, third person singular) through the washing of 'regeneration' or 'new birth' (paliggenesia, a near hapax, that is, a word that occurs only once or twice in the entire Bible) and renewing of the Holy Spirit. The explicit denial of human works as the cause and the assignment to divine mercy and the Spirit make the regenerating act monocausal (having a single cause).

God ('God', theos) is the active subject of the participle 'having begotten again' (anagennesas, a completed past action in active voice as a participle), 'having begotten us again'. The believers are the object ('us', hemas) and the ground is divine mercy. The verb 'to beget again' (anagennao) occurs only twice in the canon, both in this letter, so its sense is read mainly from this immediate context, where the agent is unambiguously God.

'Having willed it' (bouletheis, a completed past action as a participle, from 'to will', boulomai), 'he brought us forth' (apekuesen, a completed past action in active voice as a simple statement of fact, third person singular, from 'to give birth', apokueo, a birth verb used only twice, both in James). The participle of deliberate willing modifies the divine subject, so the begetting flows from God's own will and act, with the readers again as the object ('us', hemas).

Everyone who believes ('everyone the one believing', pas ho pisteuon, an ongoing-action participle in the active voice) that Jesus is the Christ 'has been begotten of God' (ek tou theou gegennetai, a completed action whose result still stands, in passive voice as a simple statement of fact). The perfect passive presents the begetting as a settled accomplished state and the believing as present, which some read as the birth grounding the faith, but the grammar states a correlation of a present state with a perfect state and does not by itself fix which is logically first.

Those who 'were begotten' (egennethesan, a completed past action in passive voice as a simple statement of fact, third person plural) were begotten 'not of bloods' (ouk ex haimaton) 'nor of the will of the flesh nor of the will of a man' (oude ek thelematos sarkos oude ek thelematos andros), but 'of God' (all ek theou, 'but from God'). Three 'from' (ek) phrases in the 'from-X' grammatical form (the genitive of source), each marking a human origin, are each negated, and the noun 'will' (thelema) is denied twice before the single positive 'from God' (ek theou). This is the clearest grammatical exclusion of human will from the new birth in the anchor set.

complicating_texts.resolution: The phrase 'born of water and Spirit' (ex hydatos kai pneumatos) is sometimes read sacramentally (treating a church rite as the means), which could appear to make a human rite the instrument of regeneration (the new birth). Lexically the verb 'might be born' (gennethe) stays a completed past action in passive voice in the subjunctive mood and the construction keeps the person as the one born, while 'water' most plausibly stands with 'Spirit' (pneuma) as a single cleansing image echoing the water and new spirit of Ezekiel 36:25-27, a link the cross-reference data confirms (John 3:5 to John 1:13 and the Ezekiel chain). The verse introduces no human causal verb, so it does not weaken the divine-agency reading.

The phrase 'through the washing' (dia loutrou, with the noun 'washing' in the 'from-X' grammatical form, the genitive) can be pressed as a baptismal-instrument argument that would make the rite the operative cause. The verse itself first denies 'works in righteousness that we did' (the verb is first person plural, 'we did') and assigns the saving to 'his mercy' and the Spirit, so even on an instrumental reading of 'washing' (loutron) the originating cause stays with God and the monocausal (single-cause) lexical pattern holds.

The verse immediately before grants the right to become children of God to those who 'received' and 'believed' ('they received', elabon, a completed past action in active voice; and 'believing', pisteuousin, an ongoing-action participle in the active voice), which can be read as faith preceding sonship and so contradicting the ordering claim. Verse 13 then grounds that same group in a birth 'not of human will but of God'. The text holds reception and divine begetting together without lexically ranking which is logically first, which is exactly why the causal-priority sub-claim is rated as inference and the overall confidence is medium.

The pairing of the ongoing-action participle 'believing' (pisteuon) with the perfect-tense 'has been begotten' (gegennetai, a completed action whose result still stands) is read by some as the new birth being settled before the believing, and by others as the present believing being the visible mark of the begetting without a stated temporal gap. The Greek tenses establish a real correlation of a present act with an accomplished state but do not by themselves order the two, so this verse is the precise locus where the words leave the 'order of salvation' (ordo salutis) open, and it is addressed here rather than resolved one way.

variants.note: No variant units were supplied in the bundle and the cited books are outside current ECM apparatus scope (the critical edition of New Testament textual variants; only 3 John is ingested for CBGM, the genealogical method used in that edition). The known transposition and punctuation discussions in John 3 do not touch the passive voice of 'to beget' (gennao) or the agency of the Spirit, and the singular versus plural reading of John 1:13 in a few witnesses does not change the negated human will and the positive 'from God' (ek theou), so the verdict is variant robust on the available evidence.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Reads the recurring passive of 'to beget' (gennao), the triple negation of human will in John 1:13, the perfect passive 'has been begotten' (gegennetai, a completed action whose result still stands, in passive voice) of 1 John 5:1, the negated 'is able' (dynamai) with the perfect-passive 'has been given' gift of John 6:65, and the dead-then-made-alive sequence of Ephesians 2:5 as establishing both sole divine agency and the logical priority of new life over faith. On this reading the perfect tense (completed-action-with-standing-result form) of being begotten functions as the standing cause behind the believing and obeying that the same passages describe.

Grants that God alone is the grammatical agent of the new birth, since the passive verbs and the divine-subject active verbs are not in dispute, but reads John 1:12, the conditional 'if' (ean) clauses of John 3 (an 'if-then' style construction), the second person response verbs of Ezekiel 36:27, and the ongoing-action participle 'believing' (pisteuon) of 1 John 5:1 as leaving the begetting and Spirit-enabled faith concurrent rather than strictly sequenced. On this reading the text affirms divine sole-agency in the birth while declining to settle the strict causal-priority of regeneration (the new birth) before faith, treating that ordering as a systematic inference the vocabulary underdetermines.

hermeneutics.notes: Both lenses agree on the agency question because the morphology (word-form analysis) is the same for both (passive 'to beget' gennao, divine-subject active verbs, the human as object). They diverge only on the ordering sub-claim, and that divergence is itself lexical in origin: the canon supplies tense correlations (present-form faith alongside completed-with-standing-result begetting) that the words relate but do not rank. The verdict affirms the proposition while marking the ordering portion as inference, which is why confidence is medium.

stem_audit.neutralized_form: The new birth is a work in which God or the Holy Spirit is the sole acting agent who imparts spiritual life to those described as dead in sin, with this divine action presented as the ground that enables saving faith.
stem_audit.notes: The term 'monergistic' (meaning 'one-working', that only one party acts) is a systematic-theology label coded to a particular tradition and is not itself a lexical datum, and the phrase 'logically prior to and the cause of saving faith' imports an 'order of salvation' (ordo salutis) ordering. The verdict was derived on the neutral substance, divine sole-agency and the enabling-then-response sequence, which the queried grammar of the anchor texts supports (passive 'to beget' gennao throughout, divine-subject active verbs, first person divine verbs ahead of second person human verbs in Ezekiel 36). The ordering sub-claim is treated as an inference drawn from the enabling texts rather than an explicit lexical statement, which is reflected in the medium confidence rating. VERDICT-CHANGED: no. Verdict unchanged from the prior file; the direct lexical queries confirmed the morphology (word-form analysis) the prior verdict assumed.

lay_summary: Looking only at the original-language words, the new-birth passages share one striking pattern. The verb for being born, 'to beget or be born' (gennao), keeps appearing in the passive voice all through John 3, so the person is born, not someone who births himself, and Jesus compares the Spirit ('wind' or 'Spirit', pneuma) to wind that blows where it wills. In John 6 the Spirit is the one that gives life ('giving life', zoopoieo) and the flesh profits nothing, and no one is able to come unless it has been given to him from the Father. Ezekiel 36 stacks up first-person verbs spoken by God: I will give (the Hebrew verb 'to give', natan) you a new heart, I will remove (the Hebrew verb 'to remove', sur, in the causative 'to cause to do' form) the heart of stone, I will put my Spirit ('spirit' or 'breath', ruach) within you, and only after those does the people's own keeping and walking follow. Ephesians 2 says God 'made us alive together with' (synezoopoieo) Christ while we were dead in our trespasses, and dead people cannot revive themselves. Titus 3 says he saved us not by works we did but according to his mercy ('mercy', eleos), through the washing of regeneration ('new birth' or 'rebirth', paliggenesia). First Peter 1 and James 1 both make God the one acting and us the ones acted upon, James adding that God 'having willed' ('to will', boulomai) 'brought us forth' ('to give birth', apokueo) because he willed to. John 1:13 is the sharpest: those born were born not of bloods, nor of the will ('will', thelema) of the flesh, nor of the will of a man, but of God (ek theou, 'from God'), three denials of human origin before one positive source. So the words consistently put all the initiative on God and the Spirit and treat the person as the recipient. That settles the agency question firmly. The further claim that this birth comes logically before faith and causes it fits the enabling language of John 6:65 and the perfect tense (a completed action whose result still stands) of having been begotten in 1 John 5:1, but those verses correlate faith and the new birth without flatly stating which is first, so that part of the claim is a reasonable inference rather than something the grammar nails down, and that is where careful readers can still differ.
